title: Pulmonary Genetics
subject: Respiratory System (RESP)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the inherited lung diseases that boards test most, cystic fibrosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and primary ciliary dyskinesia, and the acquired mutations that turn bronchial epithelium into lung cancer. Each disease is taught as a chain from gene to protein to cell to organ, because exam questions usually give the organ findings and ask for the defect, or give the defect and ask you to predict the findings. The cancer sections explain how the p53 and Rb brakes work, how tobacco carcinogens damage DNA, and why adenocarcinoma, small cell carcinoma, smokers, and never smokers carry different driver mutations.
prerequisites: Mendelian inheritance: autosomal recessive and codominant patterns, carrier probability
Protein folding, endoplasmic reticulum quality control, and the ubiquitin proteasome pathway
Epithelial ion transport: apical channels, Na+/K+ ATPase, and water movement by osmosis
Airway histology: ciliated pseudostratified epithelium, goblet cells, and mucociliary clearance
Obstructive lung physiology: elastic recoil, FEV1/FVC, and lung volumes

connections.how: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is the clearest example of the protease and antiprotease imbalance that underlies all emphysema.
The same CFTR defect that dehydrates airway mucus blocks pancreatic ducts and causes fat malabsorption and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
Retained Z alpha-1 antitrypsin is a cause of neonatal hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma.

connections.to: Embryology of body axes and the heart
connections.how: Nodal cilia set left-right asymmetry, which explains situs inversus and heterotaxy in primary ciliary dyskinesia.
The driver mutations in this chapter define the molecular subtypes of adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and small cell carcinoma.

sections.title: Cystic fibrosis: CFTR, F508del, and dehydrated mucus

blocks.text: CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator) is an apical anion channel in airway, pancreatic, intestinal, biliary, sweat duct, and male reproductive epithelium. It is an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) protein that works as a channel, not a pump. Protein kinase A phosphorylates its regulatory (R) domain, and ATP binding at two nucleotide-binding domains opens the pore. CFTR conducts chloride and bicarbonate, and in the airway it probably restrains sodium absorption through the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC).

Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive. CFTR lies on the long arm of chromosome 7, and the carrier frequency is about 1 in 25 in people of Northern European ancestry. More than 2,000 variants are known; those blocking synthesis, folding, or gating cause the most severe disease. The most common, F508del, removes three base pairs, deleting phenylalanine 508 without a frameshift. The protein misfolds, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) quality control retains it, and it is ubiquitinated and destroyed by the proteasome, so very little CFTR reaches the apical membrane. What escapes also opens poorly.

blocks.title: F508del to bronchiectasis
steps: Phenylalanine 508 deleted; CFTR misfolds in the ER
Ubiquitin tags the protein for proteasomal degradation
Little CFTR reaches the apical membrane
Chloride and bicarbonate secretion fall; ENaC uptake continues

Thick mucus traps bacteria; neutrophils accumulate
Repeated infection destroys bronchial walls: bronchiectasis
blocks.caption: A processing defect ends as structural lung damage.

blocks.text: Cilia can beat only within a periciliary liquid layer about 7 micrometers deep. When chloride secretion fails and sodium absorption continues, water follows sodium out of the airway surface liquid, the layer collapses, and mucus sticks to the epithelium. Lost bicarbonate secretion also acidifies the liquid, impairing mucin expansion and antimicrobial peptides. Trapped bacteria recruit neutrophils, whose elastase and DNA thicken the mucus and damage the bronchial wall. Staphylococcus aureus and Haemophilus influenzae dominate in childhood; mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which forms alginate biofilms, dominates in adults.

The sweat gland shows that one defect can change ion flux in opposite directions. The secretory coil produces a near-isotonic fluid, and the duct normally reabsorbs NaCl, with CFTR carrying the chloride. Without CFTR, chloride stays in the lumen and sodium cannot be absorbed without its counterion, so sweat is salty. A sweat chloride of 60 mmol/L or more supports the diagnosis; 30 to 59 mmol/L is intermediate and below 30 mmol/L makes it unlikely. Salt loss in hot weather can cause hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis in infants.

blocks.title: CFTR loss outside the lower airway
rows: Low duct fluid and bicarbonate; enzymes plug ducts
Exocrine insufficiency (about 85%): steatorrhea, vitamin A, D, E, K deficiency; high immunoreactive trypsinogen on newborn screen
Meconium ileus in about 15 to 20% of affected newborns
Vas deferens obstructed and lost in fetal life
Absent vas deferens; azoospermia, normal spermatogenesis
blocks.caption: Each finding traces to too little fluid and bicarbonate secretion.

blocks.predict: CFTR secretes chloride in the airway but reabsorbs it in the sweat duct. Predict what its loss does to chloride in each fluid.
blocks.explain: Airway secretion fails, so the surface liquid is depleted; sweat duct reabsorption fails, so chloride stays in sweat. The gradient, not the channel, sets the direction.

blocks.title: Worked example: carrier risk in a family
blocks.text: A healthy woman has a brother with cystic fibrosis; her partner, of Northern European ancestry, has no family history. Her parents are both carriers, so her genotype odds are 1/4 normal, 1/2 carrier, 1/4 affected. Because she is unaffected, the affected quarter is removed: her carrier probability is (1/2) divided by (3/4), or 2/3. Her partner carries the population risk, about 1/25. Two carriers have a 1/4 chance per child. The child's risk is 2/3 x 1/25 x 1/4 = 1/150.

sections.title: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: emphysema and cirrhosis

blocks.text: Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) is a serpin made mainly by hepatocytes and secreted into plasma, from which it diffuses into the lung interstitium and alveolar lining fluid. Its main target is neutrophil elastase. Elastase cleaves the AAT reactive loop at methionine 358 and is trapped in an irreversible complex. AAT is an acute phase protein and the main component of the alpha-1 band on serum protein electrophoresis.

The SERPINA1 gene is on chromosome 14. Alleles are named by their protease inhibitor (Pi) electrophoretic type and are codominant: both alleles are expressed, so the serum level is roughly the sum of the two contributions. M is the normal allele. S (glutamate 264 to valine) is mildly reduced. Z (glutamate 342 to lysine) is severely reduced, and null alleles make no protein.

blocks.title: Genotype, serum level, and organ risk
rows: Slightly increased with other liver injury
High: neonatal hepatitis, cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma
None, because no protein is retained
blocks.caption: Lung risk tracks low serum AAT; liver risk tracks retained Z protein.

blocks.text: Emphysema results from imbalance between proteases and antiproteases. With little AAT, elastase released by neutrophils digests elastin in alveolar walls evenly from the respiratory bronchiole to the alveolar sac, so the emphysema is panacinar, and it is worst at the lung bases, probably because blood flow, and therefore neutrophil delivery, is greatest there. Ordinary smoking-related emphysema is instead centriacinar and worst in the upper lobes. Smoking accelerates AAT deficiency in two ways: smoke recruits neutrophils and macrophages, and oxidants oxidize methionine 358, inactivating the AAT that remains. PiZZ smokers may be dyspneic by their 30s or 40s. Lost elastic recoil removes the radial traction that holds small airways open, so they collapse in expiration: FEV1/FVC falls, total lung capacity and residual volume rise, and diffusing capacity (DLCO) falls with the lost alveolar surface.

blocks.title: PiZZ to lower lobe panacinar emphysema
steps: Z protein polymerizes and is retained in hepatocyte ER
Serum AAT falls to about 10 to 15% of normal
Neutrophil elastase in the alveoli acts unopposed
Elastin destroyed across the whole acinus, worst at the bases
Lost recoil: expiratory airway collapse, air trapping, low DLCO
blocks.caption: The lung consequence is a loss of function: too little inhibitor where elastase is released.

blocks.text: The liver disease has the opposite mechanism, a toxic gain of function. The Z substitution lets the reactive loop of one molecule insert into the beta sheet of the next, forming polymers that cannot leave the ER. Accumulated polymer causes ER stress and hepatocyte death, presenting as neonatal cholestatic hepatitis or later as cirrhosis with a higher risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. On biopsy the polymers are round eosinophilic globules in periportal hepatocytes that are PAS-positive and diastase-resistant: diastase removes glycogen but not this glycoprotein. Null alleles produce no protein, so they cause emphysema without liver disease. Serum electrophoresis shows a reduced alpha-1 band, and because AAT rises with inflammation, an acute illness can push a PiMZ level into the normal range.

blocks.title: Worked example: codominance in a PiMZ family
blocks.text: Two PiMZ parents each pass M or Z with equal probability. Their children are 1/4 PiMM, 1/2 PiMZ, and 1/4 PiZZ. Because the alleles are codominant, each genotype has its own serum level: about 100%, 60%, and 10 to 15% of normal. A PiMZ child therefore has a measurable deficiency but usually no disease unless other injury such as smoking is added, while a PiZZ child is at risk for neonatal cholestasis now and panacinar emphysema later. A level alone can mislead, because inflammation and S or null alleles also change it, so Pi typing settles the genotype.

sections.title: Primary ciliary dyskinesia and Kartagener syndrome

blocks.text: Motile cilia line the airways, paranasal sinuses, middle ear, fallopian tubes, and brain ventricles, and the sperm flagellum is built the same way. All share the 9+2 axoneme: nine outer microtubule doublets around a central pair. Each doublet carries inner and outer dynein arms, ATPase motors that walk along the neighboring doublet. Nexin links tie the doublets together so that sliding is converted into bending, and radial spokes coordinate the beat. Airway cilia beat about 10 to 15 times per second in coordinated waves that carry the mucus layer toward the pharynx.

Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) is usually autosomal recessive and genetically heterogeneous, with more than 50 genes identified. The most common defects are in outer dynein arm genes such as DNAH5 and DNAI1, and electron microscopy most often shows absent or shortened outer dynein arms, sometimes with inner arm loss as well. Defects of radial spokes or the central pair also cause PCD, and some forms look nearly normal on electron microscopy, so genetic testing and high-speed video of ciliary beating complement it. Without working dynein, cilia are immotile or beat stiffly and out of phase.

Most affected term newborns have unexplained respiratory distress, and a daily wet cough and nasal congestion begin in infancy. Mucus composition is normal, but with cough as the only clearance, retained secretions and repeated infection cause chronic rhinosinusitis, otitis media with effusion and conductive hearing loss, and bronchiectasis, typically in the middle and lower lobes. Men are infertile because sperm, though normal in number, cannot swim. Women have reduced fertility and more ectopic pregnancies because oviduct cilia help move the ovum. Nasal nitric oxide is characteristically very low, a useful screening finding whose cause is not fully understood. Sweat chloride is normal, which separates PCD from cystic fibrosis.

blocks.title: Cystic fibrosis and primary ciliary dyskinesia compared
blocks.caption: Both diseases fail mucociliary clearance, so their lung disease looks alike; the extrapulmonary findings separate them.

blocks.text: Left-right asymmetry is set during gastrulation at the primitive node. Node cilia have a 9+0 axoneme but still contain dynein, so they rotate, and because they tilt posteriorly their rotation drives a leftward flow of fluid across the node. This flow triggers expression of Nodal, Lefty, and the transcription factor PITX2 on the left side, which directs heart looping and organ position. If node cilia cannot move, there is no directional cue and sidedness is decided by chance: about half of patients have situs inversus totalis, a full mirror image, and a smaller group has heterotaxy, often with congenital heart disease. Kartagener syndrome is PCD with situs inversus, giving the triad of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. Dextrocardia appears on the ECG as an inverted P wave, QRS, and T wave in lead I with R waves that shrink rather than grow from V1 to V6.

blocks.predict: Two siblings carry the same pair of DNAH5 mutations. One has situs inversus and the other has normal organ position. Predict why, and whether normal anatomy argues against PCD.
blocks.explain: Without nodal ciliary flow, sidedness is random, so each embryo has about an even chance of either arrangement. Normal organ position does not exclude PCD; only about half of patients have situs inversus.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on the primitive node and left-right asymmetry.

sections.title: p53, Rb, and how tobacco carcinogens mutate TP53

blocks.text: The cell cycle runs from G1 through S (DNA synthesis) and G2 to mitosis (M). The restriction point in late G1 commits the cell to divide without further growth factor signal. Cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) drive progression; each is active only when bound to its cyclin and is opposed by CDK inhibitors. The G1 to S transition matters most in cancer because a cell that copies damaged DNA turns the damage into a permanent mutation in both daughter cells.

Rb, the product of RB1 on chromosome 13, is the gatekeeper. Hypophosphorylated Rb binds the transcription factor E2F and recruits histone deacetylases, silencing genes needed for S phase. Growth factors induce cyclin D, which activates CDK4 and CDK6; these phosphorylate Rb and partly release E2F. E2F then induces cyclin E, which with CDK2 hyperphosphorylates Rb, a positive feedback loop that makes the switch irreversible. Freed E2F drives transcription of S phase genes such as DNA polymerase and dihydrofolate reductase. Rb is dephosphorylated after mitosis, resetting the brake.

blocks.title: Regulators of the G1 to S transition
rows: Phosphorylates Rb in response to growth factors
Binds E2F; blocks S phase genes
Senses DNA damage; arrests G1 or triggers apoptosis
Mutated (loss); the most often mutated gene in cancer
blocks.caption: All converge on Rb phosphorylation, so tumors usually disable this checkpoint at one point.

blocks.text: p53, from TP53 on chromosome 17p, is a transcription factor that responds to stress rather than driving the cycle. MDM2 normally ubiquitinates p53, keeping it short-lived. DNA damage activates the ATM and ATR kinases, which phosphorylate p53 so MDM2 cannot bind it. p53 accumulates and induces p21, which keeps Rb hypophosphorylated and holds the cell in G1, and GADD45, which aids repair. If repair fails, p53 induces BAX and PUMA and triggers mitochondrial apoptosis. RB1 and TP53 are tumor suppressors, so usually both alleles must be lost (Knudson two-hit model); missense p53 can also act as a dominant negative because p53 is a tetramer.

blocks.title: p53 and MDM2 feedback
steps: DNA damage activates ATM and ATR kinases
Phosphorylated p53 escapes MDM2 and accumulates
p53 induces p21: G1 arrest for repair
p53 also induces MDM2 transcription
After repair, MDM2 degrades p53
blocks.caption: Negative feedback: p53 induces its own inhibitor, ending arrest after repair.

blocks.text: Tobacco smoke carries more than 60 carcinogens, mainly polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons such as benzo[a]pyrene and nitrosamines such as NNK. Benzo[a]pyrene is a procarcinogen: cytochrome P450 1A1, induced by smoke through the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, and epoxide hydrolase convert it to benzo[a]pyrene diol epoxide, an electrophile that binds the N2 position of guanine. Nucleotide excision repair normally removes these bulky adducts. If they persist, the polymerase tends to place adenine opposite the damaged guanine, producing a guanine to thymine transversion in the next round of replication. In smokers' lung tumors these transversions cluster at TP53 hotspot codons such as 157, 248, and 273, the same sites where the diol epoxide preferentially forms adducts. Without p53, damaged cells keep dividing, so smokers' lung cancers carry very high mutation burdens.

blocks.title: Benzo[a]pyrene to loss of the G1 checkpoint
steps: Benzo[a]pyrene inhaled in smoke
CYP1A1 forms the diol epoxide
Epoxide binds guanine: bulky DNA adduct
Unrepaired adduct; adenine inserted opposite
Guanine to thymine transversion at a TP53 hotspot
No arrest or apoptosis; damaged cells divide
blocks.caption: Activation makes the carcinogen; failed repair and replication fix the mutation.

blocks.predict: A tumor has lost both copies of RB1. Would restoring p16 arrest it in G1?
blocks.explain: No. p16 acts upstream by inhibiting CDK4/6; with Rb gone, E2F is free regardless. p16 loss and Rb loss are alternative hits on one switch.

sections.title: Driver alterations in adenocarcinoma and small cell carcinoma

blocks.text: A driver alteration gives a tumor cell a growth advantage and is selected during tumor evolution, while passenger mutations ride along. Lung cancers are divided into non-small cell carcinomas (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, large cell carcinoma) and small cell carcinoma, and their drivers differ. Adenocarcinoma is the most common type overall and the most common in never smokers, and its drivers are mostly activating changes in the receptor tyrosine kinase to RAS pathway.

EGFR is a receptor tyrosine kinase. Ligand binding normally causes dimerization and autophosphorylation, which recruits the adaptor GRB2 and the exchange factor SOS; SOS loads RAS with GTP. RAS-GTP then activates the RAF, MEK, ERK cascade toward proliferation and the PI3K, AKT, mTOR pathway toward survival and growth. Lung cancer EGFR mutations lie in the kinase domain, mostly exon 19 deletions and the exon 21 L858R point mutation, and they keep the kinase active without ligand. In the EML4-ALK fusion, created by an inversion within chromosome 2p, the EML4 coiled-coil domain holds the ALK kinase domain in a permanently dimerized, active state. KRAS mutations, most often at codon 12, prevent GTPase-activating proteins from stimulating GTP hydrolysis, so RAS stays locked in the active GTP-bound form.

blocks.title: Where the adenocarcinoma drivers act
steps: Growth factor binds EGFR (mutant EGFR skips this step)
Kinase dimerizes and autophosphorylates (EML4-ALK does this constitutively)
GRB2 and SOS load RAS with GTP
RAS-GTP stays on (mutant KRAS resists GAP-driven GTP hydrolysis)
RAF, MEK, ERK and PI3K, AKT signal
Proliferation and survival without external signal
blocks.caption: EGFR, ALK, and KRAS activate one pathway at different levels, which explains why they rarely occur together.

blocks.text: EGFR mutations occur in about 10 to 15% of adenocarcinomas in Western populations and about 40 to 50% in East Asian populations, and are most frequent in never smokers and women. Without the tobacco mutation load, these tumors are driven by a single potent kinase mutation, which is why EGFR-mutant adenocarcinoma is the classic lung cancer of a woman who never smoked. KRAS mutations, in about 25 to 30% of adenocarcinomas in Western series, are concentrated in smokers; the common smoker variant, G12C, is a guanine to thymine transversion, the benzo[a]pyrene signature from C04. ALK fusions, in about 3 to 7%, occur in younger never or light smokers. Because these three activate the same pathway, a second one adds little advantage, and they are nearly mutually exclusive. A tumor comes to depend on its driver, termed oncogene addiction.

Small cell carcinoma, a neuroendocrine tumor almost confined to heavy smokers, is defined by loss of tumor suppressors rather than kinase activation. Biallelic inactivation of TP53 and RB1 is found in nearly all tumors, often with MYC family amplification. With both G1 brakes gone, the cells divide rapidly, with high mitotic counts and early metastasis. Squamous cell carcinoma, also strongly linked to smoking, typically shows TP53 mutation, CDKN2A (p16) loss, and gains on chromosome 3q that include SOX2.

blocks.title: Major driver alterations in lung cancer
rows: Never smoker, woman, East Asian ancestry
blocks.caption: Adenocarcinoma drivers turn the growth pathway on; small cell carcinoma removes the brakes.

integration.text: Cystic fibrosis and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency are both protein folding diseases, but they end differently. Misfolded CFTR is destroyed, so disease comes only from lost channel function in every epithelium that uses it. Misfolded Z antitrypsin escapes degradation and polymerizes, so the lung suffers a loss of function while the liver suffers a toxic gain of function. Primary ciliary dyskinesia fails the same clearance system as cystic fibrosis from the other side, the motor rather than the fluid, and its embryology explains organ reversal. All three lead to chronic neutrophil inflammation, and neutrophil elastase is the common final pathway of tissue destruction in bronchiectasis and emphysema.

Lung cancer joins biochemistry, cell biology, and pathology. Smoke carcinogens need P450 activation, their adducts need excision repair, and failed repair leaves a recognizable guanine to thymine signature in TP53 and KRAS. Tumors arising this way carry many mutations and lose the p53 and Rb brakes, whereas never-smoker adenocarcinomas usually depend on a single kinase driver. These are statistical associations, not rules: EGFR mutations occur in some smokers, KRAS mutations in some never smokers.

summary: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive (CFTR, chromosome 7); F508del misfolds and is degraded by the proteasome, so little channel reaches the membrane.
Lost chloride and bicarbonate secretion with continued ENaC sodium absorption dehydrates airway mucus, leading to infection and bronchiectasis.
In the sweat duct CFTR reabsorbs chloride, so its loss raises sweat chloride to 60 mmol/L or more.
CFTR loss also causes pancreatic insufficiency, meconium ileus, focal biliary cirrhosis, and absent vas deferens with obstructive azoospermia.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin alleles are codominant; PiZZ gives about 10 to 15% of normal serum levels, lower lobe panacinar emphysema, and cirrhosis.
Z polymers retained in the hepatocyte ER form PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules; null alleles cause emphysema without liver disease.
Primary ciliary dyskinesia removes dynein arm function, causing bronchiectasis, sinusitis, otitis, and infertility; situs is random, so about half have situs inversus.
Rb holds E2F until cyclin D with CDK4/6 phosphorylates it; p53 senses DNA damage and induces p21 to keep Rb active and arrest G1.
Benzo[a]pyrene is activated by CYP1A1 to a diol epoxide whose guanine adducts cause guanine to thymine transversions in TP53.
EGFR and ALK drive adenocarcinoma in never smokers, KRAS drives it in smokers, and small cell carcinoma loses both TP53 and RB1.

verify: Sweat chloride cutoffs (60 mmol/L or more consistent, 30 to 59 intermediate, below 30 unlikely) follow current Cystic Fibrosis Foundation diagnostic consensus; older texts use 40 to 59 as borderline.
Whether loss of CFTR increases ENaC activity in human airways is debated; current work also stresses lost bicarbonate secretion. Confirm the mechanism NABNE expects.
Approximate serum AAT levels by genotype (PiMZ about 60%, PiSZ about 40%, PiZZ about 10 to 15%) vary with assay and source.

The statement that synthesis, folding, and gating variants cause the most severe cystic fibrosis follows the CFTR functional class scheme (six classes in most sources, five or seven in some); confirm the classification NABNE uses.
Population frequencies of EGFR, KRAS, and ALK alterations vary widely by study and ancestry; figures here are approximate.
Percent of PCD patients with situs inversus (about half) and heterotaxy (about 6 to 12%) varies between series.
Confirm whether NABNE expects gene names such as DNAH5, DNAI1, PITX2, and SOX2, or only the protein and mechanism level.
